body.text: Victorian English language charity investigated over funding for white nationalist groups
In short:
An ABC NEWS Verify investigation has found the English-Speaking Union's Victoria branch provided a $2,000 grant to white nationalist publication The National Observer.
The charity also has ties to a far-right white nationalist organisation, the British Australian Community.
What's next?
The Australian English-Speaking Union has launched an investigation into the Victorian branch following questions from ABC NEWS Verify.
A national charity has launched an internal investigation into its Victorian branch after ABC NEWS Verify uncovered funding for far-right, white nationalist organisations.
The investigation began after the ABC alerted the Australian English-Speaking Union to a $2,000 grant ESU Victoria made to a white nationalist online publication called The National Observer (TNO).

In a recent anonymous article titled "Australian Remigration — What it would look like, and how it could be achieved tomorrow", TNO called for the "accelerated removal of non-citizens" and for incentivising the permanent "departure" of some Australians who hold dual citizenship.
Another recent TNO article was titled "Are White Australians being replaced? The media says it's a conspiracy theory, the data says otherwise".
The National Observer also has its own weekly podcast hosted by its founder, who goes by the name "John Lawson".
In November 2025, TNO published an interview by Lawson with Eric Orwoll, founder of US "whites only" enclave Return to the Land, about how their ideas could be used in Australia.
Australian white nationalists have also appeared as guests on the podcast and aired racist and antisemitic views during their interviews.
Building a 'young elite'
Representatives of far-right European political parties have starred as guests on The National Observer's podcast, sharing lessons on pro-nationalist politicking.

During an episode with a campaigner for German political party Alternative for Germany, or AfD, one of the Australian hosts confessed that the purpose of The National Observer was to "try and build a young elite who have these right-wing ideas", a movement they said they hoped could replicate the AfD's electoral success.
In a statement to ABC NEWS Verify, ESU Victoria defended awarding the grant to TNO.

"The National Observer's application relied on its provision of independent podcasts promoting Australian culture, heritage and language. That application sought funding for the purchase of media equipment (lapel microphones) and website development.

"While the content of the National Observer's podcasts are that organization's responsibility, we support the common law freedoms available to all Australians, including freedom of expression," the statement read.

ESU Victoria's defence appears to be out of step with the national charity parent body, ESU Australia, which told ABC NEWS Verify it took the matter seriously and had launched an internal investigation.

"AESU is a non-partisan, non-political organisation. We do not engage in political advocacy, nor do we support donations to political organisations or to any organisation that does not uphold the ESU's purpose and mission," a spokesperson told ABC NEWS Verify.

The global English-Speaking Union exists across 50 countries and was founded more than 100 years ago by British journalist Sir Evelyn Wrench, who, according to the organisation, "envisioned a world where shared language could bridge cultural divides and foster peace".
The Victorian branch's activities, many of which are aimed at young people, include rhyming poetry competitions and supporting schoolchildren to practise public speaking.
It has significant sums of money at its disposal: according to financial documents, ESU Victoria has more than $16 million in cash and assets.
The ABC does not suggest that all ESU Victoria members share or support white nationalist views.
Ties to political organisation calling for race-based deportations
ABC NEWS Verify can reveal ESU Victoria also has ties to a far-right political interest group called the British Australian Community (BAC).
The BAC says it exists to "promote and defend the interests of Anglo-Celtic Australians".
The group has engaged in white nationalist rhetoric, including advocating for remigration, which is the deportation of those of non-European heritage.
In a post on X in 2024, the BAC referenced Australian Anglo-Celtics being "under siege" by the "threat" of "mass indiscriminate immigration".

In a 2024 press release, the group referred to itself as "immigration patriots" and called on then-opposition leader Peter Dutton to "initiate the orderly remigration of recent arrivals wishing to return to their homelands".
It then explicitly called for the creation of a race-based immigration system, asking for the adoption of "immigration policies designed to cap and reduce ethnic diversity in Australia".
It also wanted a government department created to deport people.
"The British Australian Community recommends establishing a Department of Emigration responsible for managing the diplomatic and logistical dimensions of mass negative migration," the release said.
Company documents reveal the BAC and ESU Victoria share a building in Ascot Vale in Melbourne's inner North-West.
ESU Victoria president Robert Furlan was previously a secretary of the BAC.
According to a post in a BAC group on social media, since 2016, all BAC members are automatically associate members of the ESU in Victoria.
When asked about this, ESU Victoria said the BAC was historically a corporate member of ESU Victoria, but that as of 2016 all its corporate membership and associated benefits had ceased to operate.

In the past, ESU Victoria has provided funding for a BAC campaign opposing the renaming of places and monuments to recognise Indigenous heritage. It also sponsored an annual BAC event called "Britfest".
ESU Victoria told the ABC it has no current financial relationship with the BAC.

"ESU Victoria Branch and the British Australian Community are separate entities. ESU Victoria Branch has no comment to make about the BAC's website content or media statements other than to reiterate our support for common law freedoms, including freedom of expression," the ESU Victoria statement said.
Company records show that the current secretary of the BAC is Frank Salter.
Dr Salter co-founded an organisation in the 1970s called the Australian National Alliance (ANA).
Reports at the time described it as an anti-immigration group with a focus on recruiting young people.
Dr Salter later moved into academia and has written extensively on ethnicity, genetics, and "mass immigration".
In 2023, the ESU Victoria announced the awarding of a grant to Dr Salter supporting a publication titled "Collected essays on the national question".
Dr Salter's books are also advertised via Amazon affiliate links hosted on the far-right website The Noticer.
The Noticer also has published Dr Salter's opinions on race, describing him as a representative of the BAC.
ABC NEWS Verify understands Dr Salter has also been a member of ESU Victoria in the past, though it is not clear if he still is.
Dr Salter did not respond to a list of questions sent to him by ABC NEWS Verify.
Call for federal government to investigate charitable status

On its website, the ESU Victoria says it adheres to a definition of English-speaking people that is defined as "people of the British Isles and their descendants who settled in countries such as Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States of America".

Extremism researcher Josh Roose, from Deakin University, told ABC NEWS Verify that the ESU Victoria branch appeared to share some of the more "traditionalist pseudo-intellectual elements" of the far right or the extreme right.

"They believe that the English-speaking peoples, which appears to be quite narrowly defined to white countries, are people who are losing their heritage and need some sort of support to maintain that in the face of overwhelming odds," he said.
Dr Roose said some of ESU Victoria's activities — like its grant to The National Observer — risked crossing the line into funding political activism.
"[The National Observer] is an organisation that is not staffed by or run by a well-known, reputable academic base or even journalistic base. These are primarily activists,"
he said.
"When you're platforming white nationalists … there's a very, very thin line here as to what's acceptable and it certainly warrants further investigation."
Dr Roose called on the Australian government to initiate a thorough review into ESU Victoria, to investigate their stated aims, mission, and their actual activities.
"Charities are there to serve the greater good. And that's ultimately what charities are, by definition, established to do,"
he said.
"When a charity is being used and cloaked effectively in a certain language to allow it to use tax breaks … at times to achieve a political purpose, then it's moved well beyond its remit."
